content:
If you use a deprecated declaration that has been deprecated in favor of a declaration with a different type, then we already note this fact in the deprecation warning. For example, if you write

theorem bar : 2 = 2 := rfl

@[deprecated bar (since := "2026-07-24")]
theorem foo : 1 = 1 := rfl

theorem baz : 1 = 1 :=
  foo

then in addition to the recommendation you use bar, it also tells you that the types of foo and bar are different:

`foo` has been deprecated: Use `bar` instead

Note: The updated constant has a different type:
  2 = 2
instead of
  1 = 1

Recently I was surprised to see this warning because I thought I had deprecated something in favor of an identical declaration which turned out to not be identical. I am considering extending this warning (in core) to already warn about this at the moment you add the deprecated attribute. I think this might be a good idea because (1) it helps protect against accidental mis-deprecations and (2) it gives you an early idea that addressing a deprecation might me more than just a purely mechanical replacement.

To do a deprecation where the types do not match exactly (or more precisely up to reducible defeq), you would use a syntax like @[deprecated bar (since := "2026-07-24") (inexact := true)].

Of the 4210 deprecations in mathlib, 599 (15%) currently fall into this "inexact" category. From a quick look, I didn't find any that are obviously mistaken. I guess in mathlib, the "inexact" cases will be almost exactly those cases where alias is not used.

You could add a bunch of heuristics here, like not warning if the replacement is a generalization, or if the replacement is a generalization after swapping out all deprecated names in the statement for their replacements, but I think I would want to keep it simple (just like the current warning).

So, my question: what does the mathlib crowd think of this? Are the potential benefits worth typing (inexact := true) 15 percent of the time when deprecating something?

What does "identical" mean? defeq? implicit-reducibility defeq? syntactic equality? I see now that this is answered above.

The idea seems fine to me.

Snir Broshi said:

Could the syntax be +inexact?

Usually the declare_*_config_elab commands allow both automatically (unless this is defined too early to use those).

In addition to it being useful to give you visibility into what you’re doing (whether you’re replacing what you think you are, as you said), I think communicating more about how things have changed over time in source is strictly beneficial! :)

And if it comes with a code action letting you automatically insert/remove this flag as soon as the attribute recognizes it’s needed/unneeded, I imagine the chance of people complaining will be even lower :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:
Other possibilities for wording might be newType or typeChanged, if inexact is too inexact about what part of the declaration is not exactly the same :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

Just to sound a note of caution: what will be the expectations upon PR authors/reviewers once this new tool is available? I.e., if we have a tool which highlights any deprecation that isn't exact up to reducible defeq, then should PR authors be required to ensure this doesn't trigger (or to provide elaborate justifications why the typeChanged flag is being used)?

("Tools" become "rules" very easily around here, given mathematicians' innate pedantry and love for order. I suspect that as soon as the technology is there to highlight non-exact deprecations, reviewers will start treating them as errors to be fixed.)

What concerns me is that this much stronger requirement would end up making refactoring jobs harder. E.g., if we have two lemmas which say exactly the same thing but with the arguments in a different order, or otherwise use an obviously equivalent but not quite reducibly-defeq formulation, then that would result in a warning. This would end up being an incentive against refactors to remove code duplication and/or improve consistency of related statements, which hitherto we have generally regarded as a Good Thing.
I will make sure that the warning message is clear that it is perfectly fine to have mismatched types if that is intentional.
